title: Number of Students Unable to Eat Lunch
description: Simulate a cafeteria queue where students only take a sandwich matching their preference, reduced to a two-counter counting problem.

sections.title: Number of Students Unable to Eat Lunch

content.title: Number of Students Unable to Eat Lunch

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

The school cafeteria offers circular and square sandwiches, represented by 0 and 1. Students stand in a queue, each with a preference (0 or 1) given in students, and sandwiches are stacked with the top sandwich at sandwiches[0]. Each turn, the student at the front of the queue looks at the top sandwich: if it matches their preference, they take it and leave; otherwise, they go to the back of the queue without eating. This repeats until no remaining student wants the top sandwich. Return the number of students left unable to eat.

blocks.caption: Count preferences, then consume the sandwich stack while a matching student remains.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Details"],"rows":[["Input","students[] (0/1 preferences, front is students[0]), sandwiches[] (0/1, top is sandwiches[0])"],["students.length == sandwiches.length","Same number of students as sandwiches"],["Stop condition","A full pass through the current queue with no one taking the top sandwich"],["Output","Number of students still in the queue when the process stops"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

The queue-and-cycle simulation is the literal description, but the key insight is that a student's identity and original position never matter, only their preference type (0 or 1). Since the queue only ever cycles students who do not match, once neither remaining preference type matches the top sandwich, the process is stuck forever. This turns a positional queue simulation into a simple counting problem.

blocks.title: Connection
blocks.text: Similar to problems like Design Circular Queue in that a queue is the surface-level structure, but the real state that matters collapses down to just two counters.
3. Understand the Problem

Picture a cafeteria line. The server holds up the next sandwich. Whoever is at the front either grabs it (if it matches what they want) or steps to the back of the line. If everyone remaining in line has already refused the current sandwich once (a full lap with no match), no one will ever take it, and service stops there.

blocks.caption: Service halts as soon as everyone left in line has refused the current sandwich.

items: Only two preference values exist, 0 and 1, so track counts of each rather than tracking individual students.
The sandwich stack is consumed strictly from the top, in order.
The process stops the moment the count of students wanting the current top sandwich type reaches zero.

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
students = [1,1,1,0,0,1], sandwiches = [1,0,0,0,1,1]. Initial counts: 2 students want 0, 4 want 1.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Top sandwich","Matching count before","Action","Counts after"],"rows":[["1","want1 = 4","Matched, served","want0 = 2, want1 = 3"],["0","want0 = 2","Matched, served","want0 = 1, want1 = 3"],["0","want0 = 1","Matched, served","want0 = 0, want1 = 3"],["0","want0 = 0","No one wants it, STOP","want0 = 0, want1 = 3"]]}

blocks.title: Answer
blocks.text: The stack still has 3 more sandwiches (0, 1, 1) after service stops, but they are irrelevant since no one left in line wants a 0. The answer is want0 + want1 = 0 + 3 = 3, matching the expected output.
5. How Should We Think?

The direct simulation literally moves a queue and a stack: pop the front student, compare to the top sandwich, either serve or requeue, and detect a stall by counting consecutive non-matching rotations equal to the queue size.

Since student identity is irrelevant, replace the queue with two counters, one per preference type. Walk the sandwich stack top to bottom; while the current sandwich type still has a waiting student (counter > 0), decrement that counter. The instant a sandwich type has zero waiting students, the process is permanently stuck, since every remaining student wants the other type and it never appears again until deeper in the stack, if at all, and even then would face the same problem in reverse.
6. Brute Force Solution

Simulate directly with a queue of students and a stack of sandwiches. Track how many consecutive rotations happened without a match; if that count ever reaches the current queue size, everyone left has refused, so stop.
7. Analyze the Brute Force

blocks.content: {"headers":["Metric","Value","Why"],"rows":[["Time","O(n^2) worst case","Each rotation is O(1), but up to n rotations can happen before every stall detection, and removing from the middle of the sandwich list is O(n)"],["Space","O(n)","Queue and stack copies of the input"]]}

blocks.title: Bottleneck
blocks.text: Explicitly rotating a queue of students to detect a stall does unnecessary work: the stall condition only depends on the two preference counts, never on the order students were requeued in.
8. Optimize the Solution

Count how many students want 0 and how many want 1. Then walk the sandwich stack from top to bottom: for each sandwich type, if the matching count is already 0, stop immediately since the process is stuck; otherwise decrement that count. The final answer is the sum of both remaining counts, since every student left is unable to ever be served.

items: Build want[0] and want[1] by counting students, O(n).
Walk sandwiches once, decrementing the matching counter or breaking out, O(n).
No actual queue rotation is needed since order among same-preference students never matters.

10. Complexity Comparison

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","Time","Space"],"rows":[["Brute Force, queue and stack simulation","O(n^2)","O(n)"],["Optimized, two counters","O(n)","O(1)"]]}

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: When only a small, fixed set of values matter, replace a queue simulation with counters over those values.
A stall condition based on "no one left wants this" is naturally detected by a counter hitting zero, no rotation tracking needed.
This is a good example of recognizing that a problem's literal description (queue, stack) is not the same as its minimal necessary state.

blocks.text: 12. Final Summary

Number of Students Unable to Eat Lunch collapses a queue-and-stack simulation into two counters, one per preference type. Walking the sandwich stack once and decrementing the matching counter (or stopping the moment it hits zero) finds the answer in O(n) time and O(1) extra space, since a stalled preference type can never recover once the other students exhaust that type from the front of the queue.
